chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
title: Frankie Trumbauer's Tiger Rag solo and playing on changes
summary: They discuss Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo that saxophonists admired, and that playing on changes was around early.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: The fact that Trumbauer didn't really swing much -- I mean he -- when he played something in a tempo of like 'Singing the Blues' it didn't matter too much. But on other tempos there seems to be a funny kind of rhythm there. It sounds a little corny.
That didn't matter too much apparently in the way he was appreciated anyhow.
I remember a place -- I don't know what the name of it was but it was based on 'Tiger Rag' that Frankie Trumbauer played and it was a real great solo.
And all the saxaphone players dug it. You know. It went like this -- (singing). You remember that one?

That's Trumbauer -- I don't know whether it's his or not, but he didn't sound -- he sounded as modern in them times. Frankie did -- that sounds good now you know when you play it. So what are you going to do with that?

That's playing with a lot of -- you know -- with a lot of changes, so that was already pretty much a way of playing then. Some times people seemed to think that playing on changes didn't come in until later on, but it was there --
Sure. That song they sung in Virginia" was real great, you know.
Uh-huh. Musicians listen to those records a lot I guess.
